section: Dinewan the Emu, and Goomblegubbon the Bustard
body: And ever since that time a Dinewan, or emu, has had no wings, and a Goomblegubbon, or bustard of the plains, has laid only two eggs in a season.

_provenance.author: K. Langloh Parker
_provenance.caution: PROTOCOL-SENSITIVE VOICE, NOT YET CLEARED FOR PRODUCTION. No consent grant / elder sanction exists for elder_of_country as of 2026-08-18 (checked scripts/, scripts-resilience/). Parker was a European settler folklorist recording without the consent frameworks used today; this passage was selected as a non-ceremonial nature/animal-origin narrative, but selection by an AI is not a substitute for community review. GOVERNANCE.md requires elder sanction as a deployment condition for this voice before any content -- however innocuous-seeming -- is approved or embedded.

body: And there, if you look, you may see the seven sisters together. You perhaps know them as the Pleiades, but the black fellows call them the Meamei.

_provenance.author: K. Langloh Parker
_provenance.caution: PROTOCOL-SENSITIVE VOICE, NOT YET CLEARED FOR PRODUCTION. The Seven Sisters / Pleiades narrative is one of the most widespread Aboriginal story complexes across Australia and has documented restricted/gendered dimensions in many traditions even where public tellings also exist -- this specific telling reads as a public 'why' story in Parker's text, but that judgment has not been made by anyone with standing in the tradition. See dream-alt-001 note.

section: The Galah, and Oolah the Lizard
body: You Oolah shall carry bindeahs on you always, and the stain of my blood.

source: More Australian Legendary Tales (K. Langloh Parker, 1898)
body: A good spirit who lived in the sky saw how bright and beautiful the earth looked when lit up by this blaze. He thought it would be a good thing to make a fire every day.

_provenance.author: K. Langloh Parker
_provenance.caution: PROTOCOL-SENSITIVE VOICE, NOT YET CLEARED FOR PRODUCTION. Sun-origin narratives are significant Dreaming content in many Aboriginal traditions; whether this particular telling is appropriate for broad sharing is a determination for a community elder, not an AI selecting for apparent innocuousness. See dream-alt-001 note.

source: More Australian Legendary Tales (K. Langloh Parker, 1898)
body: The crane woke up at last, and when he opened his mouth to yawn he felt like choking. And to this day the only noise a crane can make is, 'gah-rah-gah, gah-rah-gah!'

body: The next name of connection is local, based on belonging to one country or hunting-ground; this name a child takes from its mother wherever it may happen to be born.

_provenance.author: K. Langloh Parker
_provenance.caution: PROTOCOL-SENSITIVE VOICE, NOT YET CLEARED FOR PRODUCTION. Ethnographic description of kinship structure, not narrative -- selected as general/non-ceremonial, but see dream-alt-001 note; kinship and naming systems can carry protocol dimensions not visible to an outside reader.

body: So relationships are always kept in their memories by being daily used as names.

_provenance.author: K. Langloh Parker

body: In hearing the old blacks tell their legends you notice a great difference between them as raconteurs -- some tell the bare plot or feature of the legend, others give descriptive touches all through.

_provenance.author: K. Langloh Parker
_provenance.caution: PROTOCOL-SENSITIVE VOICE, NOT YET CLEARED FOR PRODUCTION. Uses period-typical racialized language typical of 1905 ethnography ('the old blacks') which would itself need editorial handling before any public-facing use, separate from the ceremonial-content question. See dream-euah-001 note.
